summary: Color is a numeric attribute that ties a traffic engineering tunnel or policy to an intent, such as low latency. This document extends PCEP so that the color can be carried between path computation elements and clients.

eli5.summary: Color-coding your lunch boxes tells you what is inside. A route can be tagged with a color for what it is good at, such as fast or cheap, and PCEP can now carry that tag.

questions: what is color in traffic engineering
what is the pcep color tlv
how is color used in traffic engineering
subtitle: A small PCEP extension that lets a PCE and its clients carry the 32-bit color of a TE tunnel or policy.

tldr.problem: A traffic engineering tunnel or SR Policy can be tagged with a color that stands for an intent such as low latency, but PCEP had no way to carry that color for stateful PCE paths.
tldr.mechanism: A new capability flag (bit 20) is advertised in the STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV, and a new COLOR TLV (type 67) in the LSP object carries the 32-bit color value.
tldr.outcome: PCEs and PCCs can assign and report a color on any stateful TE path, except SR paths that use the SR Policy Association of RFC 9862, which already encode color.

today: RFC 9863 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025 and has not been obsoleted or updated. For SR paths that use the SR Policy Association, color is carried as described in RFC 9862 instead.

sections.title: Color for TE Paths
sections.content:
Color is a 32-bit unsigned integer that ties a Traffic Engineering (TE) tunnel or SR Policy to an intent or objective. For example, a tunnel built for low latency can carry a color that stands for "low latency". The color then guides how services are mapped onto the tunnel.

The word has nothing to do with the "thread color" of RFC 3063 or the "resource color" (link color) used in several TE routing RFCs.

The RFC builds on RFC 8231 (stateful PCE), RFC 8281 (PCE-initiated LSPs) and RFC 8664 (SR paths). How a PCC uses color to map services is out of scope.
sections.eli5: A color is a label saying what a route is good for, like a sticker on a lunch box.

sections.title: Advertising Color Capability
sections.content:
When a PCEP session starts, each speaker sends an Open message whose OPEN object holds the STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV from RFC 8231. This document defines a new flag in that TLV, the C-bit (bit 20), which a PCE or PCC sets to say it supports color.

A speaker that advertised color capability MUST NOT send the COLOR TLV to a peer that has not advertised it.
sections.eli5: Before using stickers, each side says whether it understands them.

sections.title: The COLOR TLV
sections.content:
The COLOR TLV is carried in the LSP object of PCRpt, PCUpd and PCInitiate messages. Its type is 67 and its length is 4. The value is a 4-byte unsigned integer, and zero is allowed.

The TLV MAY be present, and only one SHOULD be included. If it appears more than once, only the first is processed and the rest MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: The sticker is a number that fits in four bytes. Zero is a fine number too.

sections.title: Rules and Error Handling
sections.content:
The extension MUST NOT carry color for SR paths set up with the SR Policy Association of RFC 9862, because that association already includes the color. A speaker with both capabilities MUST NOT send the COLOR TLV for SR paths, and a COLOR TLV that arrives in a message with an SR Policy Association is ignored; the association's color takes precedence.

If a PCC cannot honor a color in a PCUpd or PCInitiate message, it MUST reject the message with a PCErr of Error-Type 19 (Invalid Operation) and Error-value 31 (Invalid color). One example is a PCC that does not support color zero for a given path setup type.

LSPs of the same TE tunnel in one Path Protection Association Group (RFC 8745) are expected to share a color. If a speaker finds them inconsistent, it MUST reject the message with Error-Type 19 and Error-value 32 (Inconsistent color).
sections.eli5: If a router cannot use a sticker, it says so. Routes that back each other up must wear the same sticker.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The TLV and the flag add no security concerns beyond those of RFC 5440, RFC 8231 and RFC 8281. An unauthorized PCE could maliciously give an LSP the wrong color, and the procedures of RFC 8253 and RFC 9325 can protect against that.

Implementations SHOULD let the operator turn color capability advertisement on and off, and SHOULD allow configuring color for a TE tunnel or SR Policy and including it in the data model used to read operational state. No extra liveness detection is needed.
sections.eli5: A stranger could put the wrong sticker on a route, so use a secure connection.

fields.name: Color
fields.desc: Unsigned integer color value; zero is allowed.
